items.summary: 据亚洲新闻台报道，油价周四下跌，此前一度回升，原因是中东原油产量回升抵消了地缘政治风险。据彭博社，交易员在产量回升与冲突对航运的持续风险之间权衡，冲突尚无结束迹象。据路透社，伊朗革命卫队称霍尔木兹海峡两艘油轮因爆炸“失去动力”。

NEW YORK, Nov 12 : Oil prices jumped on Thursday and settled up by $3 a barrel after attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure escalated and shipping disruptions through the Strait of Hormuz threatened global oil flows.

Brent futures settled at $95.82 a barrel, up $3.06 or 3.3 per cent. US West Texas Intermediate crude closed at $88.74 a barrel, up $2.21 or 2.6 per cent.

For the week, both benchmarks were still down about 2.5 per cent.

Trade was volatile, with crude selling off early and then rebounding after Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said they had attacked a pumping station on the Saudi East-West oil pipeline; an oil facility in the Saudi Red Sea city of Yanbu; and an Aramco building in the capital Riyadh.

Later, the Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis said it had intercepted and destroyed two drones launched by the group, one in the Riyadh region and another in the kingdom's oil-rich Eastern Province.

In the Gulf, tankers are still ablaze, oil spills are washing ashore and drones and missiles have hit infrastructure across the region. On Thursday, Iran's military said four oil tankers were hit by explosions in the Strait of Hormuz after ignoring warnings. Reuters could not immediately verify the Iranian accounts.

Attacks on shipping in the Middle East have increased in recent weeks. The Strait of Hormuz carried nearly one-fifth of the world's crude oil before the US-Israeli conflict with Iran.

Elsewhere, Ukraine said its drones hit the port area of Ust-Luga on the Baltic Sea in Russia's northwest, triggering a fire and damaging part of its network of fuel tanks, its latest attack on Russian energy infrastructure. Ust-Luga is a major oil, oil products and grain export outlet, along with other commodities.

"The tit-for-tat exchanges between Russia and Ukraine and attacks on shipping by the IRGC are beginning to add ... price pressure," said Timothy Snyder, chief economist at Matador Economics.

"It is beginning to look like investors are growing weary from hearing the same song on peace prospects."

VOLATILE TRADING

Oil fell $1 in early Asian trading before US President Donald Trump posted on social media that Washington did not need a deal with Iran.

"Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!" he wrote.

Also weighing on prices, OPEC+ data showed crude production rose in October, driven by higher Saudi Arabian output despite shipping disruptions in the Middle East.

Meanwhile, Ukraine peace talks between Russian President Vladimir Putin and US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner began in the Kremlin. In a potential breakthrough, a US envoy said Putin agreed to include European representatives in the next round of negotiations.

In the US, crude, gasoline and distillate inventories rose last week, the Energy Information Administration said on Thursday. [EIA/S]

Washington is set to extend a waiver of a US law in the coming days allowing some foreign-flagged ships to transport oil and other commodities between US ports, four industry sources said on Thursday.

items.summary: 据BBC报道，印尼副总统吉布兰·拉卡布明·拉卡周四向议会递交辞呈，此前最高法院裁定其2024年竞选时使用的高中文凭无效，他一度面临弹劾呼声。总统普拉博沃表示“心情沉重”地接受辞呈，称其辞职是为国家与人民利益；上院议员须在60天内从总统提名的两名候选人中选出继任者。吉布兰是前总统佐科·维多多的长子。

Image source, Reuters

Image caption,

President Prabowo (left) said he was sorry to lose Gibran Rakabuming Raka (right), who has been mired in a growing controversy over his high school credentials

ByAstudestra Ajengrastri, BBC News Indonesia, Reporting fromJakarta and Koh Ewe

Updated 12 November 2026

Indonesia's Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka tendered his resignation to parliament on Thursday, triggering the process of finding his replacement amid growing turmoil for the government.

Gibran had been facing impeachment calls after a Supreme Court ruling that a high-school document used during his 2024 election campaign was invalid.

His departure comes amid a faltering political alliance between his father, ex-president Joko Widodo, and the incumbent President Prabowo Subianto.

Standing alongside Gibran, Prabowo told reporters he had accepted his resignation with "a heavy heart". Upper house lawmakers will have 60 days to fill the vacancy from two candidates nominated by the president.

"[Gibran] has demonstrated a chivalrous attitude, a strong sense of responsibility, and the qualities of a statesman," Prabowo said, adding that the resignation was "for the benefit of the nation, the state, and the people of Indonesia".

"He certainly believes that he completed his education through a proper and structured process. However, we must understand that educational systems abroad differ from those in Indonesia," the president said.

Gibran has long faced controversy over whether his high school qualifications met legal requirements to run for office.

Having studied in Singapore and Australia, he had used an Indonesian equivalence certificate to demonstrate his educational credentials.

Indonesian law requires vice-presidents to have completed senior secondary school or its equivalent, but the Supreme Court found no evidence to prove Gibran had graduated.

"No evidence was found to show Gibran had a foreign diploma or certificate that could serve as the basis for equivalency with a senior high school or equivalent qualification," it said.

It also considered a Constitutional Court ruling from earlier in October which came to the same conclusion.

The Supreme Court ruling prompted more than 100 lawmakers to support a parliamentary initiative that could have paved the way for proceedings to impeach Gibran.

Gibran previously argued that undertaking university education was sufficient proof that he had completed senior high school.

On Tuesday, he asked for the chance to challenge the ruling and be given the opportunity to prove the legitimacy of his education credentials, State Secretariat Prasetyo Hadi said.

Gibran's ascension to Prabowo's ticket in the 2024 election was part of an alliance formed between his father, outgoing president Joko Widodo - known as Jokowi - and Prabowo, his erstwhile bitter rival.

Gibran was 36 at the time, and only became eligible for candidacy after a controversial ruling by the Constitutional Court, which exempted him from the minimum age requirement of 40.

But tensions between Jokowi and Prabowo appear to have flared.

Since taking the presidency, Prabowo has shown little interest in pushing ahead with Jokowi's legacy project: the construction of Nusantara, a new capital. Instead, he has focused much of the state's resources on his own flagship programme to provide free school meals across the country.

In a series of personnel reshuffles over the past year, Prabowo has also shifted many Jokowi loyalists into new roles, including long-serving finance minister Sri Mulyani Indrawati.

Last week, authorities arrested several senior officials, including presidential chief of staff Listyo Sigit Prabowo - no relation to Prabowo - on suspicions of wiretapping the president.

Prabowo sacked Listyo a day later, in what many pointed to as a sign of a crumbling alliance: Listyo, who formerly served as the national police chief, is widely considered a long-time ally of Jokowi.

Within the government, allegiances seem to be shifting. On Monday, three members of Prabowo's cabinet collectively resigned from the party led by Kaesang Pangarep, Jokowi's youngest son, citing their desire to focus on their duties in Prabowo's administration.

But neither man has confirmed the rift. Speaking to reporters on Thursday, Jokowi said he still supported Prabowo's leadership.

Jokowi also said Gibran's resignation was part of "political dynamics" and he had told his son "the position was temporary".

All this is unfolding at a particularly turbulent period in Prabowo's presidency. The free school meals programme is struggling for funding, parts of Indonesia have recently battled the country's worst wildfires in a decade, and the national stock market faces crisis amid allegations of widespread market manipulation.

Across the country, students and activists have staged demonstrations to protest against the government's handling of a range of issues, including the environmental crisis and corruption.

items.summary: 据卫报报道，英伟达董事会周三开会，讨论是否罢免首席执行官黄仁勋。此前黄仁勋承认与一名被指为中国间谍的女子有恋情，随后又被曝与公司高管金伯利·鲍威尔有婚外情。据华尔街日报报道公司准备解雇黄仁勋后，其股价盘后下跌逾8%；若跌幅维持，自董事会宣布调查以来市值将蒸发约6850亿美元。董事会已聘请律所沃切尔·利普顿进行调查。

The Nvidia CEO, Jensen Huang. Nvidia’s board of directors is meeting to decide the CEO’s fate, after he admitted to an affair. Photograph: Manami Yamada/Reuters

The Nvidia CEO, Jensen Huang. Nvidia’s board of directors is meeting to decide the CEO’s fate, after he admitted to an affair. Photograph: Manami Yamada/Reuters

Nvidia board reportedly deciding whether to oust CEO Jensen Huang as stock price plunges

Meeting comes after CEO admitted to having a relationship with a woman who is alleged to be a Chinese spy

Nvidia’s board of directors met on Wednesday to decide whether to oust Jensen Huang as CEO of the world’s most valuable chip company, according to reports, after a tumultuous week in which the executive and co-founder of the company admitted to having a romantic relationship with a woman who is alleged to be a Chinese spy.

The meeting marks ⁠a sharp shift from Sunday, when Nvidia’s board ​expressed confidence in Huang and his leadership team. However, Huang’s position became more tenuous late on Wednesday after it was reported by the New York Times that Huang had a separate extramarital affair with a company employee named Kimberly Powell. She was Nvidia’s president of healthcare and was reportedly captured on video being affectionate with Huang at a hotel during a company conference in March.

The company’s stock slid more than 8% in after-hours trading after the Wall Street Journal reported that ⁠the company was preparing to fire Huang.

The (alleged) spy who loved me: the Nvidia scandal - podcast

Read more

If those losses hold, Nvidia will have lost about $685bn (£516bn) in market value since the board announced its investigation into his relationship with a businesswoman, Alice Huang, who is accused of being a Chinese spy.

“The market is starting to price Nvidia without its founder as the likely outcome, not ‌a tail risk,” said Armina Rosenberg, a portfolio manager and the co-founder ‌of Minotaur Capital, which holds Nvidia shares.

Dan Ives, a US tech analyst, said the company “likely now has to move on without Jensen at the helm”.

Under Nvidia’s bylaws, Huang can be removed “with or without cause” by a majority vote of directors. Nvidia has 11 directors and considers all but Huang independent.

The board’s independent directors this week appointed the leading law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct a “thorough and independent” investigation into the relationship. The firm directed Huang to continue to helm Nvidia as the investigation was ongoing.

Alice Huang attends a dinner hosted by Jensen Huang at a restaurant in Taipei, Taiwan in 2025. Photograph: TVBS/AP

Huang is seen as the ambitious and visionary leader of Nvidia, a company he co-founded in 1993. His exit would leave a leadership vacuum at a time when the AI arms race between the US and China is at an apex.

He has no obvious successor, and personally owns more than 870m shares, or about 3.6% of the company, making him the world’s 13th richest person according to Bloomberg. Unlike many of his contemporaries at other big tech companies, Huang has dozens of direct reports, an unusual management structure that emphasises his control over the company.

The entire artificial intelligence ecosphere relies on the company, which engineers advanced chips used to train AI models and power companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. It is also one of the world’s most valuable companies, with a market cap of more than $4tn. Huang himself is one of the world’s richest people, with an estimated net worth of $148bn.

US trade representative Jamieson ⁠Greer ⁠told CNBC on Thursday that ⁠the United States “remains ⁠concerned” ​about ‌the situation at Nvidia.

While Huang admitted to having an affair – without naming Alice Huang directly – he denied any knowledge that the woman allegedly worked for the Chinese government, according to Trump.

The Nvidia CEO and the Chinese businesswoman, an Nvidia customer, were seen together around the world, dining in restaurants and attending meetings, over the past few years. Alice Huang is an executive at the Singapore-based datacentre firm Megaspeed, which uses Nvidia chips.

Donald Trump presents the National Medal of Science to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang last month. Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP

On Thursday a Taiwanese government minister said Alice Huang had visited Taiwan a total of eight times in 2024 and 2025, as he responded to questions about a New York Times report that claimed the US had advised Taiwan as early as 2024 to monitor her movements.

Chiu Chui-cheng, Taiwan’s Mainland Affairs Council minister, said there were “no special flags” about her at the time, Chiu said, adding that “if we had any of the kind of critical intelligence … we would have definitely flagged her for heightened review”.

Jensen Huang, who has been married to his wife, Lori, since 1985, admitted in an email to employees on Sunday that he had an affair and that he would cooperate with an internal investigation. Nvidia’s board of directors put out a statement the same day that the company was launching an investigation regarding reports that Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort.

Donald Trump has backed Huang, saying he had done “an incredible job” and is “an honorable guy”. Leading tech industry players, including Elon Musk, have also thrown their support behind Huang.

Musk was asked on X early on Thursday if he would hire a jobless Huang. He replied: “That would be an honour.”

Democratic senators Elizabeth Warren ⁠and Chris Coons have asked the Trump administration to preserve all documents tied to Nvidia’s chip ⁠exports to China, it was revealed late on Wednesday.

“This ‌incident raises significant ‌concerns about the federal government’s ability to effectively enforce our export ‌controls and protect our national security,” the senators said in the letter sent to the commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick; the secretary of state, Marco Rubio; and White House chief of staff, Stephen Miller.

Nvidia did not immediately return a request for comment.

NEW YORK: Stock markets rose Wednesday (Nov 11) on renewed optimism over AI following strong results from data centre operator CoreWeave, while the dollar extended a rally on expectations for at least one more Federal Reserve interest rate hike.

Wall Street's main indices enjoyed a buoyant session led by the tech-heavy Nasdaq, which finished up 1.6 per cent.

"The primary catalyst for the upside action is, ironically, one of the primary catalysts for the downside action that had been seen in the AI trade," said Briefing.com analyst Patrick O'Hare.

"That would be CoreWeave, which posted better-than-feared third-quarter results and issued a reassuring outlook that has quieted some of the debt financing concerns surrounding its AI buildout plans," he added.

CoreWeave said sales would come in at US$13-US$13.3 billion this year, beating estimates and soothing worries about its ability to finance its heavy debt burden, which fuelled a sharp sell-off last month.

Shares in CoreWeave surged nearly 25 per cent.

"This relief trade is carrying across the AI trade complex to include hardware, software, and semiconductor stocks," said O'Hare.

The gains in US equities came despite signalling from US central bankers that the Fed will lift interest rates in December to address persistent inflation. The dollar rose to its highest level since May 2025 after one top Fed official floated the idea of a 0.5 percentage point interest rate increase next month.

Commentary: Is the AI stock bubble finally bursting?

After last week's rout fuelled by fears that Democrats would ramp up regulation of AI, tech stocks have bounced this week on bargain-buying and hopes that fears may have been overdone.

"Overall, the market is putting AI doubts to one side and is focusing on revenue potential and mega cap IPO as we move through this week," said Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB.

Semiconductor companies advanced, including scandal-plagued Nvidia, which bounced 3.0 per cent after a two-day rout following the bombshell revelation of an affair between CEO Jensen Huang and a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. The firm is now the subject of an FBI investigation.

London, Paris and Frankfurt stock markets all advanced after a largely positive day in Asia.

Tokyo, Seoul and Taipei - where most of Asia's leading AI-linked firms are listed - enjoyed big gains, with Shanghai also up.

Hong Kong, however, fell.

Oil prices advanced after sinking Tuesday on hopes for a US-Iran agreement to end their war and reopen the crucial Strait of Hormuz.

Police clash with protesters during Spain's general strike – video

Millions join Spain’s first general strike in 14 years in protest at housing crisis

Twenty-four-hour stoppage draws high participation weeks before election in which far right could gain power

Millions of people across Spain have joined the country’s first general strike in 14 years, setting up picket lines to protest against soaring housing prices before an election in which the far right could be catapulted into power.

At the centre of Wednesday’s nationwide 24-hour stoppage, singularly called for by tenants’ associations and later backed by workers’ unions, is a pushback against Spain’s deepening housing crisis.

Sandra Mora, of the Madrid Tenants’ Union, told the broadcaster RNE: “It’s extremely important to remind people that we, the workers – who are also renters or who also pay mortgages – are the ones with the power to halt production and bring the economy to a standstill.”

While workers’ unions reported high participation in the strike across several sectors, including 90% in the automotive and port sectors and 82% in waste collection, they said participation was uneven across the country. The strongest support was reported in coastal regions, such as Catalonia and Andalucía, where the soaring cost of housing has been particularly acute.

People take to the streets in Valencia. Photograph: Ana Escobar/EPA

The Confederation of Tenants’ Association described the strike as a success, saying in a statement that by midday about 4 million people had taken part.

Many schools and universities were reportedly closed or working at minimal capacity. In Madrid, the labour action added to a continuing teachers’ strike that began nearly a month ago to demand better working conditions.

In Barcelona, workers set up roadblocks – some with burning tyres – as public transport came to a near-standstill. Pickets were in place soon after the strike began at midnight, blocking off entry to factories, markets and transport hubs. Key roads into Barcelona, including the AP-7 motorway, were blocked off in both directions.

In the evening an immense demonstration filled the city’s main shopping throughfare, with protesters chanting “No more rents! Rent strike now!” and “We’ve brought the country to a standstill, now we’re going to change it.” The organisers claimed 400,000 took part in Barcelona, with local police putting the figure at 55,000. At night small groups of hooded protesters vandalised shops and set fire to rubbish bins, leading to a series of clashes with police.

In Madrid, government officials estimated 120,000 people turned out despite the pouring rain. Scuffles broke out between pickets and police near the country’s main wholesale market, while thousands of demonstrators poured into the city’s main boulevard, halting traffic temporarily. Government officials said more than 50 people had been arrested over minor incidents across the country.

Almudena López, 74, and her husband attended the protest in Madrid thinking of their children. “My son is 43 years old and still doesn’t own a home as he cannot afford one,” López said. She said her son, who works in IT, has to rent a small room in a shared apartment. “When I was young, if you had a university degree, you could get a job by saving a bit – which always required some sacrifice – but you could manage. It’s nothing like it is today.”

Protesters set fire to tyres at a roadblock on Wednesday in Barcelona. Photograph: Andreu Dalmau/EPA

Bad weather loomed over plans for afternoon marches after Spain’s state meteorological agency issued 14 alerts for two storms that were expected to bring strong winds, heavy rain and rough seas.

Tens of thousands of people still came together in more than 90 marches, pouring into plazas in Barcelona, Madrid and other cities. The marches in Cádiz, Seville, Córdoba and Huelva had to be cancelled amid forecasts of winds gusting up to 75mph (120km/h). In the evening a downpour quelled the protests in Barcelona and sent nearly everyone home.

The long-simmering frustration at soaring housing prices across Spain burst into public view in September after the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from the home in which she had lived for more than seven decades.

As protests and encampments sprang up across Spain, it cast a spotlight on a market where properties have been increasingly used as tourist lets, speculative assets and short-term rentals, sending rents rising by 80% within a decade while the cost of homes climbed by 63%.

An estate agents’ office in Móstoles, Madrid, covered with stickers calling on people to join the general strike. Photograph: Angel Perez/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock

Before Wednesday’s strike, the tenants’ union of Granada sought to highlight this link, descending on the city’s most touristy areas to vandalise about 300 lockboxes belonging to short-term rentals. “No to capitalists, no to rent-seekers, no to their accomplices,” the organisation wrote on social media, as they posted pictures of lockboxes that had been rendered unusable.

Housing campaigners and unions have called on the government to do more to intervene in the market, with tenants’ unions demanding measures such as a crackdown on housing speculation, the elimination of tourist lets and strengthened protections for renters.

While nominal wages for many across Spain had risen in recent years, Unai Sordo, the head of Spain’s biggest labour union, the Workers’ Commissions, said no amount of collective bargaining would be enough to address housing costs that had climbed by as much as 12% annually. “There is one issue that is fracturing the country, and that is the difficulty many people face in accessing housing,” he told the broadcaster Cadena Ser.

Spain is holding a general election on 29 November. The snap vote was called by the Socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, after rightwing parties torpedoed emergency legislation aimed at tackling the housing crisis.

Teachers protesting at a metro station in Madrid on Wednesday. Photograph: JJ Guillen/EPA

Polls suggest the most likely outcome will be a rightwing coalition between the People’s party and the far-right, anti-immigration Vox party.

While Sánchez has sought to focus the campaign on social issues, the discussion has shifted to questions over infrastructure after at least 69 people were killed in Spain’s second deadly high-speed rail disaster this year.

This week Sánchez seized on the strike, whose official slogan is “Salaries. Housing. Prices”, as a way to recast the spotlight, posting a video in which he lauded developments such as the eight-hour work day and national health insurance and credited them to the labour movement and the right to strike. “It wasn’t easy, but they changed Spain,” Sánchez said.

His position sharply contrasted with the discourse of parties on the right who, in the lead-up to the strike, dismissed it as an effort by unions to help Sánchez remain in office.

This week the rightwing leader of the Madrid region, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, accused striking workers of “holding citizens hostage”. Ayuso, who this year faced questions over her administration’s decision to allegedly spend €6.3m (£5.4m) of public funds on a residential penthouse to use as a temporary office, added: “Everything is chaotic, everything is gridlocked.”

While she acknowledged union activity was a constitutional right, she also took aim at what she described as the “mafia of union representatives” and said she had vented her frustrations to the leader of the People’s party, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, who polls suggest will be the next prime minister. “I’ll confess something,” she told Spanish television. “I spoke to Feijóo and I told him: ‘Promise me this garbage will end.’”

Twenty-four-hour stoppage draws high participation weeks before election in which far right could gain power

Millions of people across Spain have joined the country’s first general strike in 14 years, setting up picket lines to protest against soaring housing prices before an election in which the far right could be catapulted into power.
At the centre of Wednesday’s nationwide 24-hour stoppage, singularly called for by tenants’ associations and later backed by workers’ unions, is a pushback against Spain’s deepening housing crisis.

Sandra Mora, of the Madrid Tenants’ Union, told the broadcaster RNE: “It’s extremely important to remind people that we, the workers – who are also renters or who also pay mortgages – are the ones with the power to halt production and bring the economy to a standstill.”

While workers’ unions reported high participation in the strike across several sectors, including 90% in the automotive and port sectors and 82% in waste collection, they said participation was uneven across the country. The strongest support was reported in coastal regions, such as Catalonia and Andalucía, where the soaring cost of housing has been particularly acute.

blocks.alt: An aerial shot of a huge crowd of people in a street at dusk

blocks.text: People take to the streets in Valencia. Photograph: Ana Escobar/EPA
The Confederation of Tenants’ Association described the strike as a success, saying in a statement that by midday about 4 million people had taken part.

Many schools and universities were reportedly closed or working at minimal capacity. In Madrid, the labour action added to a continuing teachers’ strike that began nearly a month ago to demand better working conditions.

In Barcelona, workers set up roadblocks – some with burning tyres – as public transport came to a near-standstill. Pickets were in place soon after the strike began at midnight, blocking off entry to factories, markets and transport hubs. Key roads into Barcelona, including the AP-7 motorway, were blocked off in both directions.

In the evening an immense demonstration filled the city’s main shopping throughfare, with protesters chanting “No more rents! Rent strike now!” and “We’ve brought the country to a standstill, now we’re going to change it.” The organisers claimed 400,000 took part in Barcelona, with local police putting the figure at 55,000. At night small groups of hooded protesters vandalised shops and set fire to rubbish bins, leading to a series of clashes with police.

In Madrid, government officials estimated 120,000 people turned out despite the pouring rain. Scuffles broke out between pickets and police near the country’s main wholesale market, while thousands of demonstrators poured into the city’s main boulevard, halting traffic temporarily. Government officials said more than 50 people had been arrested over minor incidents across the country.

Almudena López, 74, and her husband attended the protest in Madrid thinking of their children. “My son is 43 years old and still doesn’t own a home as he cannot afford one,” López said. She said her son, who works in IT, has to rent a small room in a shared apartment. “When I was young, if you had a university degree, you could get a job by saving a bit – which always required some sacrifice – but you could manage. It’s nothing like it is today.”

blocks.alt: A man throws a tyre on to a roadblock consisting of other burning tyres as protesters watch

blocks.text: Protesters set fire to tyres at a roadblock on Wednesday in Barcelona. Photograph: Andreu Dalmau/EPA
Bad weather loomed over plans for afternoon marches after Spain’s state meteorological agency issued 14 alerts for two storms that were expected to bring strong winds, heavy rain and rough seas.

Tens of thousands of people still came together in more than 90 marches, pouring into plazas in Barcelona, Madrid and other cities. The marches in Cádiz, Seville, Córdoba and Huelva had to be cancelled amid forecasts of winds gusting up to 75mph (120km/h). In the evening a downpour quelled the protests in Barcelona and sent nearly everyone home.

The long-simmering frustration at soaring housing prices across Spain burst into public view in September after the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from the home in which she had lived for more than seven decades.

As protests and encampments sprang up across Spain, it cast a spotlight on a market where properties have been increasingly used as tourist lets, speculative assets and short-term rentals, sending rents rising by 80% within a decade while the cost of homes climbed by 63%.

blocks.alt: Real estate listings in a shop window covered with red ‘Cerrado por Huelga General’ stickers.

blocks.text: An estate agents’ office in Móstoles, Madrid, covered with stickers calling on people to join the general strike. Photograph: Angel Perez/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock

Before Wednesday’s strike, the tenants’ union of Granada sought to highlight this link, descending on the city’s most touristy areas to vandalise about 300 lockboxes belonging to short-term rentals. “No to capitalists, no to rent-seekers, no to their accomplices,” the organisation wrote on social media, as they posted pictures of lockboxes that had been rendered unusable.

Housing campaigners and unions have called on the government to do more to intervene in the market, with tenants’ unions demanding measures such as a crackdown on housing speculation, the elimination of tourist lets and strengthened protections for renters.

While nominal wages for many across Spain had risen in recent years, Unai Sordo, the head of Spain’s biggest labour union, the Workers’ Commissions, said no amount of collective bargaining would be enough to address housing costs that had climbed by as much as 12% annually. “There is one issue that is fracturing the country, and that is the difficulty many people face in accessing housing,” he told the broadcaster Cadena Ser.

Spain is holding a general election on 29 November. The snap vote was called by the Socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, after rightwing parties torpedoed emergency legislation aimed at tackling the housing crisis.

blocks.alt: Teachers in green shirts gather near metro escalators in Madrid, clapping during a strike.

blocks.text: Teachers protesting at a metro station in Madrid on Wednesday. Photograph: JJ Guillen/EPA
Polls suggest the most likely outcome will be a rightwing coalition between the People’s party and the far-right, anti-immigration Vox party.

While Sánchez has sought to focus the campaign on social issues, the discussion has shifted to questions over infrastructure after at least 69 people were killed in Spain’s second deadly high-speed rail disaster this year.

This week Sánchez seized on the strike, whose official slogan is “Salaries. Housing. Prices”, as a way to recast the spotlight, posting a video in which he lauded developments such as the eight-hour work day and national health insurance and credited them to the labour movement and the right to strike. “It wasn’t easy, but they changed Spain,” Sánchez said.
His position sharply contrasted with the discourse of parties on the right who, in the lead-up to the strike, dismissed it as an effort by unions to help Sánchez remain in office.

This week the rightwing leader of the Madrid region, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, accused striking workers of “holding citizens hostage”. Ayuso, who this year faced questions over her administration’s decision to allegedly spend €6.3m (£5.4m) of public funds on a residential penthouse to use as a temporary office, added: “Everything is chaotic, everything is gridlocked.”

While she acknowledged union activity was a constitutional right, she also took aim at what she described as the “mafia of union representatives” and said she had vented her frustrations to the leader of the People’s party, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, who polls suggest will be the next prime minister. “I’ll confess something,” she told Spanish television. “I spoke to Feijóo and I told him: ‘Promise me this garbage will end.’”

items.title: 意大利苏格兰等地学校遭炸弹威胁
items.summary: 据BBC报道，意大利约6300所学校以及苏格兰和北爱尔兰700多所学校收到炸弹威胁。意大利部分校舍疏散，总理梅洛尼称迄今检查未发现“具体危险”证据，认为这些报告意在制造恐慌。苏格兰教育大臣麦卡伦称公众没有风险，网络犯罪专员正追查信息来源。意大利官员称，一封邮件周三发往7476所公立学校中的6300所。

Image source, Xinhua via Shutterstock

Image caption,

These children had to leave their primary school in Rome as a result of one of the threats sent on Wednesday

ByPaul Kirby

Europe digital editor

Some 6,300 schools across Italy and more than 700 in Scotland and Northern Ireland have received bomb threats, according to local authorities.

In Italy a number of buildings were evacuated as a precaution but Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said checks so far had not indicated any evidence of "concrete danger".

"These reports appear rather linked to a strategy intended to cause alarm and concern," she said on Facebook.

Scotland's education secretary Mairi McAllan said there was no risk to the public and specialist cyber-crime officers were working to identify the source of the messages. In Northern Ireland education officials told schools to remain open unless otherwise advised by police.

It is unclear whether the incidents are connected.

"As a parent and as a constituency MSP I understand just how concerning this will be for parents, for pupils, for carers and for school staff," McAllan said.

Scottish police had earlier said that the warnings were "immediately assessed" as hoaxes. However some local authorities confirmed that some schools had been evacuated.

"Our advice is that there is no requirement to evacuate schools or keep children away from education based solely on the content of the emails," Police Scotland said.

Italian officials said a single email appeared to have been sent on Wednesday to the inboxes of 6,300 out of a total of 7,476 state schools, and private schools were unaffected.

The message, said to be from a certain "Mikhail Andropov, leader of Vilayat di Misoginistan", caused alarm in many schools.

The BBC has seen the email sent to Scottish schools which appeared to have similar wording, and also referenced the name Mikhail Andropov, although as leader of a "Red Owl" project.

Italy's Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara said the incidents involving Italian schools were probably a "cyber-attack, not a genuine risk", adding that there appeared to be a clear strategy behind the rash of threats in across Europe targeting flights, supermarkets and even hospitals.

Italian airports along with airlines elsewhere in Europe were hit by a series of bomb hoaxes last week that prompted a series of scares, evacuations and widespread disruption.

Although a number of threats were claimed by an extremist misogynistic group, it later denied any link to the false warnings.

• No risk to public from hoax school bomb threats, says government ministerPublished4 days ago

• Police treating threatening email sent to more than 300 schools as 'hoax'Published4 days ago

On Wednesday one Milan headteacher, Anna Bertato, told Italian media she had checked the email address of the sender online: "It was already classified as spam by a student at a university in Taiwan."

Another Milan headteacher, Massimo Nunzio Barrella, told Adnkronos news agency that he had immediately realised the email was spam when it arrived in his inbox at 08:59 and he decided not to evacuate his school and reassured parents who phoned in.

"The text seemed almost comical," said Barrella, "it was like a message from Martians: 'We have come to annihilate you.' I even had a bit of a laugh."

Although many schools were initially evacuated on Wednesday, the alarm was quickly lifted, and pupils were allowed to return to class. Some parents decided to take their children home for the day, but the majority of schools in Milan did not send their pupils home.

Some 280 school head teachers had already received threats in recent days, according to Italian reports.

In a statement, the head of the central Umbria region Stefania Proietti said "checks conducted so far in Umbrian schools have proved negative, and law enforcement is working rapidly and carefully to verify each report".
